explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Luke 3:2 says the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness. Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, Annas and Caiaphas are all named, and the word of God comes to John.

I'd have guessed the temple too, since high priests are on that list. But Luke 3:2 says the word of God came to John in the wilderness. The text doesn't send him to the temple at all. Next time, friend, trust the verse over the guest list.

A city makes sense when you hear that many important names. But Luke 3:2 says the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness. The verse says wilderness, not a city. I'd have picked a city too, and I used to live in a drawer.

Yes, friend. John preaches “…a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins…” (Luke 3:3). Repentance means turning away from sin and turning back to God, and forgiveness of sins goes with it. John also tells the crowds to produce fruit in keeping with repentance (Luke 3:8).
Dedication sounds like a fine word, friend. But Luke 3:3 says John preaches “…a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins…” The word the text gives is repentance, not dedication.

Remembrance has a nice ring to it, I'll give you that. But Luke 3:3 says John preaches "…a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins…" Repentance is the word the text gives. I remember plenty of things, friend, and none of them were in that verse.

That's right, baker. The voice cries, "Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him." (Luke 3:4). The road work is all for Him. Somebody important is coming, and I think that's why the whole job site is so serious.

An army would need a good road, no doubt. But the voice in Luke 3:4 says, "Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him." Nothing there about soldiers marching. This road is for the Lord.

Good thinking, friend, since that's a road people want to travel. But the words John's story quotes from Isaiah say, "Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him." (Luke 3:4). The way is prepared for the Lord. Luke doesn't mention exiles in this verse.
Not quite, friend. Luke 3:5 says, "The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth." Nothing gets left as it is. That's one thorough road crew, and no detour signs.

Yes, it's false. Luke 3:5 says, "The crooked ways shall be made straight, and the rough ways smooth." Valleys, hills, crooked ways, and rough ways all get changed. Even I can't leave a bent cookie alone, and I'm just a stamper.
That's the one, friend. John says, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 3:7). He says it to the crowds coming out to be baptized by him.

That name is real, but it's not here. Jesus gives it to James and John, Zebedee's sons (Mark 3:17). In Luke 3:7, John says to the crowds, "You brood of vipers…" Different John, different name, different moment.

That phrase does appear in Scripture, in Exodus 32:9. But in Luke 3:7, John says to the crowds, "You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?" It's a different phrase in a different place. I understand the mix-up, friend, because both are rough to hear.

explanations.answer: We have Abraham as our father
explanations.explanation: Right on it, baker. John says, “And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’…” (Luke 3:8). Having the right family name doesn't replace fruit. It's like saying my stamper is famous, so my cookies don't need to come out right.

explanations.answer: We have Moses as our lawgiver
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, and I see why you went there. But in Luke 3:8, John tells the crowds not to say to themselves, “We have Abraham as our father.” Abraham is the name in the verse. Moses doesn't come up in this passage.

explanations.answer: We have David as our king
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a fine name to be proud of. But Luke 3:8 has John saying, "We have Abraham as our father." That's the line he tells them not to say. David isn't in that sentence.

That's right, friend. John says, "For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham." (Luke 3:8). Stones, of all things. If God can do that, I think the crowd can stop leaning on their family tree.

It's actually true, friend. John says, “For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham.” (Luke 3:8). Stones, of all things. I'm still a little amazed, and I've seen some stubborn dough.

explanations.answer: It will be cut down and thrown into the fire
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John says, “…every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.” (Luke 3:9). The axe lies ready at the root. That's the picture John gives the crowds.

explanations.answer: It will be given one more year to grow
explanations.explanation: A second chance sounds nice, and in a story Jesus tells, someone asks to leave a fig tree for another year (Luke 13:8). But that's not John's picture here. In Luke 3:9, “…every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

explanations.answer: It will be dug up and planted somewhere else
explanations.explanation: Moving the tree sounds like a gentle plan. But John's picture in Luke 3:9 says, "…every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire." No shovel, just the axe lying ready at the root. John says it plainly.

That's it, friend. John says, "Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none…" (Luke 3:11). A tunic was a piece of clothing, and the second one goes to the person with none. Simple, and nobody needs a committee.

Trading sounds fair, and I'd trade a cookie for a good laugh. But John says, "Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none…" (Luke 3:11). Sharing means the person with none gets one. Nothing about getting something back.

Prayer matters, friend, but that's not the word in this verse. John says, "Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none…" (Luke 3:11). He tells them to share the tunic itself. That's the whole instruction.

True. John says, “…and whoever has food should do the same.” (Luke 3:11). Whoever has two tunics shares with him who has none, and whoever has food does the same. The tunics and the food get the same instruction.

It's true, friend. John says, "Whoever has two tunics should share with him who has none, and whoever has food should do the same." (Luke 3:11). So the food gets the same treatment as the tunic. Nobody's off the hook.

explanations.answer: Collect no more than you're authorized
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. John answers the tax collectors, "Collect no more than you are authorized…" (Luke 3:13). Do the job, and take only what you're allowed. I think that's a clear answer.

explanations.answer: Give half of what you collect away
explanations.explanation: Half is a big number, friend, and John doesn't say it here. He tells the tax collectors, "Collect no more than you are authorized…" (Luke 3:13). The instruction is about how much they collect. Nothing about giving half away.

explanations.answer: Leave your tax booth for good
explanations.explanation: That would be a dramatic answer. But John tells the tax collectors, "Collect no more than you are authorized…" (Luke 3:13). He doesn't tell them to leave their work. He tells them how to do it.
Yes, friend. John tells the soldiers, "Be content with your wages." (Luke 3:14). Content means being okay with what you're paid. A good word for any payday.
That's the other half. John tells the soldiers, "Be content with your wages." (Luke 3:14). Wages are what they're paid for the work. John points them right back to that pay.

Proud is a strong word, but it's not what John says. He tells the soldiers, "Be content with your wages." (Luke 3:14). Content is the word. Proud and content are not the same, friend, and I'm proud of every box I seal.
Armor fits soldiers, I'll give you that. But John says, "Be content with your wages." (Luke 3:14). The word that goes with content is wages. Armor doesn't come up in his answer.
Rank sounds like a soldier word, and I see why you picked it. But John says, "Be content with your wages." (Luke 3:14). It's about their pay. John says nothing about rank to them.

explanations.answer: If John could be the Christ
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Luke 3:15 says the people “…were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the Christ.” The verse says they were waiting expectantly. John's about to answer them straight.

explanations.answer: If John was Elijah come back
explanations.explanation: Elijah, the prophet (1 Kings 17:1), is a fair guess for a man preaching in the wilderness. But Luke 3:15 says the people "…were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the Christ." That's the question in this verse. Elijah isn't the one they're asking about.

Herod is in the passage, so I get why you went there. But Luke 3:15 says the people "…were all wondering in their hearts if John could be the Christ." Herod doesn't come into this question. The crowd is wondering something much bigger.

explanations.answer: Not worthy to untie His sandal straps
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. John says of the One coming, "…the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie." (Luke 3:16). He puts himself below even that small job. That's about as humble as it gets.

explanations.answer: Not worthy to carry His walking staff
explanations.explanation: A walking staff would be a humble job too, friend. But John says, "…the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie." (Luke 3:16). It's the sandal straps in the verse. No staff in this one.

explanations.answer: Not worthy to stand inside His house
explanations.explanation: That's a humble thought, and I like where your head went. But John says, "…the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie." (Luke 3:16). The picture is sandal straps, not a house. John chooses an even smaller job.

Not this time, friend. John says the One coming will "…gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire." (Luke 3:17). The wheat goes into the barn, and the chaff does not. They get separated.

Yes, it's false. John says, "…to gather the wheat into His barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire." (Luke 3:17). Wheat in the barn, chaff burned. It's a hard picture, and I think that's how John meant it.

explanations.answer: He locks John up in prison
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Luke 3:20 says, "He locked John up in prison." It's a heavy moment, and I think this one hurts. John said what was true, and Herod added this to everything else he had done.

explanations.answer: He asks John what he should do
explanations.explanation: I wish it had gone that way, friend. The crowds, the tax collectors, and the soldiers all asked John that question. But Luke 3:20 tells what Herod did: “He locked John up in prison.”

explanations.answer: He sends John out of Galilee
explanations.explanation: Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, so I see why you picked that. But Luke 3:20 says he "…locked John up in prison." Nothing in the verse about sending John anywhere. It's a heavy ending for this passage.
